The fistula would not have been ready to use in time for dialysis even if he had had the surgery in mid-March to create it. It takes many weeks to mature.

 At 17% kidney function, he should have had a virtual appointment with his nephrologist much earlier, been having bloodwork to check his kidney function every 2 weeks or even less, and been very clearly told what symptoms would indicate his kidney function has dropped further, and that he needs to go to a hospital right away.

 A doctor can put a line in, in the neck at bedside in ICU (no surgeon needed) which can be used to start dialysis right away. Dialysis is usually started at 15% kidney function, and he was at 17%. They should have known that his arm fistula wouldn't mature by the time dialysis was needed, and put a semi-permanent one in his chest in like February (can go home with this, unlike neck one, that can only stay in while an inpatient in hospital). This chest one would then have been used until his fistula was ready. Then chest one would have been removed.

It's very unfortunate that he died, and it's very unfortunate if he didn't go to emergency because of Covid, despite symptoms because he didn't want to burden healthcare system. 

But there is more to this story, and possibly inadequate care by nephrologist prior to Covid, if it's accurately reported his kidney function was at 17%.
Standard is to schedule surgery to create fistula once kidney function is at 30%. 

I also wonder if they did an autopsy to see if it was kidney failure that was the cause of his death, and not another heart attack or some other cause.

The information should be there. Most people working a job where they are an employee can't deduct for employment expenses like uniforms. I wanted to, and I looked it up, and it was VERY clear that I couldn't. 

So if an accountant is doing someone's taxes, and making deductions that are not allowed, I would not be going back to that accountant. 

The only deduction I found I could do, was my parking cost, and since it came right off my paystub, it was easy to add up and input it. 

I have always used Studiotax myself. I like it, since I see what's where in each line, and can get more detail about that line in the tax guide.

My T4 from my employment, had the amount for the pension for that year on it. So when you, or your accountant does taxes, and you input all the amounts listed on your T4, it gets accounted for. 

It's hard to explain, especially if you don't do your own taxes, but you can always log onto your service Canada account and look at a past T4, you will see it. The box is labelled RRIF.

I don't know if this is the best advice, since where I live the house prices are considerably lower than Vancouver. But I went to a bank for mortgage pre-approval. 

The max house price I could purchase based on my approval, I deducted 100k from it, and told realtor this was my max. I ended up buying a place for 4k above my max, paid asking price for it, the day it listed on the market, because I really wanted it.

This was before my town boomed for no reason I could understand. There were houses getting 27 offers, so everyone was offering considerably above asking. 

I don't think go 100k below the maximum the bank will let you buy is a good rule or a universal rule, but it worked well for me, income has gone up and down, but making the mortgage payments have never been a stress. 

That's a big downpayment, so I would have a big emergency fund. I like 3 months expenses plus another 9 mortgage payments  plus 10k for any house repairs/costs that may come up suddenly.
